name: Lucky Array
description: Petya loves lucky numbers. Everybody knows that lucky numbers are positive integers whose decimal representation contains only the lucky digits 4 and 7 . For example, numbers 47 , 744 , 4 are lucky and 5 , 17 , 467 are not. Petya has an array consisting of n numbers. He wants to perform m operations of two types: add l r d — add an integer d to all elements whose indexes belong to the interval from l to r , inclusive (1 ≤ l ≤ r ≤ n , 1 ≤ d ≤ 10 4 ) ; count l r — find and print on the screen how many lucky numbers there are among elements with indexes that belong to the interval from l to r inclusive (1 ≤ l ≤ r ≤ n ) . Each lucky number should be counted as many times as it appears in the interval. Petya has a list of all operations. The operations are such that after all additions the array won't have numbers that would exceed 10 4 . Help Petya write a program that would perform these operations.
input_specification: The first line contains two integers n and m ( 1 ≤ n , m ≤ 10 5 ) — the number of numbers in the array and the number of operations correspondingly. The second line contains n positive integers, none of which exceeds 10 4 — those are the array numbers. Next m lines contain operations, one per line. They correspond to the description given in the statement. It is guaranteed that after all operations are fulfilled each number in the array will not exceed 10 4 .
output_specification: For each operation of the second type print the single number on the single line — the number of lucky numbers in the corresponding interval.

sample_testcases.input:
3 6
2 3 4
count 1 3
count 1 2
add 1 3 2
count 1 3
add 2 3 3
count 1 3

approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 121E — Lucky Array [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
